Adrenal Glands|Bone Marrow.description: The Adrenal Glands-Bone Marrow axis is mediated by the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, where adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) stimulates the adrenal glands to produce glucocorticoids [1]. In response to stress or inflammation, ACTH is released from the pituitary gland and binds to its receptor on the surface of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs), which then release CXCL12/CXCR4 signaling molecules that attract hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) to the adrenal glands, forming extramedullary hematopoietic niches [1]. This axis is also influenced by the presence of fluoride, which can damage the adrenal glands, but is repaired by extracellular vesicles derived from bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells [3]. Adrenal Glands|Brain.description: The Adrenal Glands-Brain axis is mediated by the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, which responds to stress signals from the brain by releasing cortisol and other glucocorticoids [1]. These hormones interact with the brain's orexin system, influencing appetite, sleep, and autonomic function, as well as modulating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, which regulates blood pressure and electrolyte balance [2]. Angiotensin II receptor signaling plays a crucial role in this axis, particularly after spinal cord injury or chronic stress, where it affects endocrine and immune function [2,3]. The HPA axis also interacts with other pituitary axes, such as the thyroid and gonadal axes, to regulate energy handling and metabolism [1].

Adrenal Glands|Kidney.description: The adrenal glands and kidneys communicate through a complex axis involving cortisol, aldosterone, and renin-angiotensin system (RAS) activation [1]. Cortisol produced by the adrenal glands stimulates the release of renin from the kidneys, which in turn activates the RAS, leading to increased blood pressure [2]. In contrast, low levels of vitamin D have been linked to impaired adrenal function and kidney disease, suggesting a potential role for vitamin D in regulating this axis [1]. The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis also plays a crucial role in modulating the relationship between the adrenal glands and kidneys, with glucocorticoid therapy affecting HPA axis activity in kidney transplant recipients [4].

Adrenal Glands|Liver.description: The adrenal glands and liver are interconnected via a complex axis involving key signalling molecules such as ghrelin and corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH). The activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis by CRH from the liver triggers the release of cortisol from the adrenal glands, which in turn affects metabolic processes [1,3]. Chronic stress can exacerbate hepatic steatosis and activate the HPA axis, leading to increased glucocorticoid production and contributing to metabolic disorders [2,3]. The interplay between these organs is crucial for maintaining homeostasis and responding to physiological and pathological stimuli.

Adrenal Glands|Muscle.description: The adrenal glands and muscles interact through the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, which is sensitive to glucose levels [1]. In response to stress or energy depletion, the HPA axis stimulates glucocorticoid production in the adrenal glands, leading to increased gluconeogenesis and lipolysis in skeletal muscle [3]. Testosterone deficiency, as seen in testicular dysfunction, triggers compensatory testicular adaptation (CTA) in the adrenal gland, resulting in increased steroid hormone synthesis [2]. Activation of the HPA axis also promotes glucocorticoid-responsive gene expression in skeletal muscle, contributing to muscle atrophy and cachexia in cancer patients [3].

Adrenal Glands|Pancreas.description: The adrenal glands and pancreas communicate through hormonal signals to regulate metabolic homeostasis. The adrenal glands produce cortisol, which stimulates the pancreas to release glucagon, a hormone that raises blood glucose levels [1]. In response, the pancreas releases insulin in an attempt to lower blood glucose, but chronic hypercortisolemia can lead to pancreatic fat deposition and impaired insulin secretion, contributing to type 2 diabetes [1]. The interplay between cortisol and insulin also affects kidney function, with cortisol promoting sodium retention and insulin reducing it, highlighting the complex endocrine axis between these organs [2].

Adrenal Glands|Small Intestine.description: The Adrenal Glands-Small Intestine axis is mediated by key signalling molecules and mechanisms that involve the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. The HPA axis is activated by stress, leading to increased production of corticosterone, a glucocorticoid hormone produced by the adrenal glands [3]. This hormone is also produced in the small intestine, where it regulates gut homeostasis and modulates the gut microbiome through interactions with the enteric nervous system [1]. Alterations in the HPA axis function, such as those induced by high-fat diets or sleep deprivation, can disrupt this axis, leading to changes in gut health and behavior [2,4].

Adrenal Glands|WAT.description: The Adrenal Glands-WAT (Wheatgerian Adipose Tissue) axis is mediated by the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, where glucocorticoids produced by the adrenal glands regulate adipose tissue compartments. The specific depot of adipose tissue influences the effects of glucocorticoids, with epicardial adipose tissue and visceral fat being key players in this process [1]. Leptin, a hormone secreted by adipose tissue, also plays a crucial role in regulating body temperature through hypothalamus-adrenal medulla-adipose tissue crosstalk [5], while glucocorticoid receptors and hydroxysteroid 11-beta dehydrogenases (HSD11Bs) are essential for the regulation of glucocorticoid action in both tissues [4]. The interplay between these molecules and mechanisms underlies the complex relationships between the adrenal glands, adipose tissue, and the HPA axis.

Bone Marrow|Brain.description: The Bone Marrow–Brain axis is a complex inter-organ communication network where bone marrow-derived cells and signaling molecules interact with the brain to regulate inflammation, metabolism, and tissue repair. In ischemic stroke, post-injury inflammation is regulated by meningeal lymphatic vessels and glymphatic transport [1], while chronic stress induces glioma growth through macrophage-mediated crosstalk between bone marrow and brain [2]. Repeated head impacts establish a senescent cranial bone marrow niche that impairs brain metabolism [3], whereas platelet-rich plasma-primed exosomes from bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells promote nerve regeneration via the miR-29a-3p/PTEN/PI3K/Akt/mTOR axis after spinal cord injury [4]. These findings highlight the critical role of bone marrow-derived signaling molecules and cells in modulating brain function and disease.

Bone Marrow|Small Intestine.description: The bone marrow-small intestine axis is mediated by inter-organ communication through the gut microbiome and hormonal signaling pathways. The gut microbiota influences bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) via modulation of connexin43 expression, which in turn affects adipose tissue homeostasis [2]. Fusobacterium nucleatum, a gut microbiota component, synergizes with BMSCs to drive colorectal tumorigenesis through Wnt3a signaling [1]. Additionally, the gut-bone axis is regulated by dietary fibers that modulate the gut microbiome and regulatory T cells, influencing hematopoietic stem cell transplantation outcomes [3].

Bone Marrow|Spleen.description: The Bone Marrow-Spleen axis is a complex inter-organ communication network that involves the exchange of signalling molecules and metabolic byproducts between these two critical organs in the immune system. The key players in this axis include ferritin, which is taken up by macrophages in bone marrow and spleen, leading to ferroptosis [4], while ATP synthase activity, regulated by ATPIF1 [3], influences mitochondrial metabolism and erythropoiesis in bone marrow. The activation of reticuloendothelial system (RES) in lymphoma patients leads to increased 18F-FDG uptake in spleen and/or bone marrow, which can serve as a prognostic marker [1]. Non-canonical NF-κB signaling, disrupted by NIK deficiency [2], plays a crucial role in thymic reconstitution and secondary lymphoid organ development.

Brain|Small Intestine.description: The brain-small intestine axis is mediated by the gut-brain axis, where the gut microbiota produces metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids [1] that are detected by the vagus nerve and released into the bloodstream, ultimately reaching the brain via the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. The gut microbiota also influences the production of neurotransmitters, such as serotonin and dopamine, through the tryptophan-kynurenine pathway [3], which is linked to Parkinson's disease pathophysiology. Furthermore, the gut-lung-brain axis plays a role in Clozapine-associated pneumonia, highlighting the interconnectedness of these organs [2]. The gut microbiota also modulates inflammation and oxidative stress, as seen in fibromyalgia, where canagliflozin has been shown to attenuate Parkinson's disease symptoms by targeting the gut-inflammasome-brain axis [3].

Brain|Spleen.description: The brain-spleen axis is a complex interplay between the central nervous system (CNS) and the spleen, mediated by key signalling molecules such as cytokines, chemokines, and neurotransmitters [1]. The gut microbiota plays a crucial role in modulating this axis, influencing the production of hormones and neurotransmitters that regulate splenic function and immune response [1]. Disruption of the brain-spleen axis has been implicated in various neurological disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, where impaired communication between the CNS and spleen may accelerate disease progression [2]. The spleen itself acts as a peripheral immune organ, sensing and integrating circulating signals to regulate immune responses, with regulatory T cells playing a key role in modulating this process [4].

Brain|Thyroid.description: The brain-thyroid axis is regulated by a complex interplay of hormonal and metabolic signals, with thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) from the pituitary gland stimulating the release of triiodothyronine (T3) and thyroxine (T4) from the thyroid gland. These hormones then bind to nuclear receptors in neurons, influencing gene expression and neuronal function [5]. Environmental toxins such as H. pylori infection [1] and exposure to flame retardants like PBDEs [2] can disrupt this axis by altering cortisol and TSH levels, leading to changes in hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis activity and potentially contributing to neurodevelopmental disorders. Disruption of thyroid hormone signaling has also been linked to neuronal apoptosis and neurotoxicity, highlighting the importance of maintaining normal thyroid function for brain health [3].

Colon|Small Intestine.description: The Colon–Small Intestine axis is mediated by a complex interplay between metabolic and hormonal signals, with key players including short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) produced by the gut microbiota [1]. The gut microbiome influences oxygen homeostasis in the gut, modulating epithelial function and immune balance through mechanisms involving spatial and developmental oxygen gradients [3]. Furthermore, the gut microbiota plays a crucial role in arsenic detoxification, with alterations in gut microbiota composition associated with long-term groundwater arsenic exposure [4]. The gut microbiome also influences liver health, with ciwujianoside B alleviating cholestatic liver injury through regulation of trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) synthesis via remodeling of the gut microbiota [5].

Heart|Kidney.description: The Heart-Kidney axis is a complex interplay of metabolic and hormonal signals between the heart and kidneys, mediated primarily by the renin-angiotensin system (RAS) [1]. Activation of RAS in the kidneys leads to increased production of angiotensin II, which stimulates sympathetic nerve activity, including renal sympathetic overdrive, as assessed by 131I-MIBG imaging [3]. This sympathetic activation can contribute to cardiac dysfunction and vice versa, forming a vicious cycle that exacerbates both heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and chronic kidney disease (CKD). The use of sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2Is), which have been shown to mitigate renal damage without adverse cardiac effects [5], may provide a therapeutic strategy to break this axis.

Heart|Liver.description: The Heart-Liver axis is a complex interplay between metabolic dysfunction and organ-specific signaling pathways. In non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy [1], liver fibrosis and fatty liver disease contribute to cardiac remodeling through the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, which activates the NF-κB pathway in cardiac tissue. Conversely, the gut-liver-heart axis is also implicated in coronary artery disease, where chronic metabolic dysbiosis leads to increased circulating ATP from hepatic ischemia-reperfusion [4], driving macrophage inflammasome activation and remote cardiac injury. Dietary omega-3 fatty acids have been shown to exert protective effects on both cardiac and hepatic function, potentially mitigating the impact of these signaling pathways [3].

Heart|Lung.description: The heart-lung axis is intricately linked through the release of key signaling molecules such as apelin [4], which plays a crucial role in regulating pulmonary vascular tone and right ventricular function [3]. The activation of soluble guanylate cyclase by vericiguat [5] also modulates atrial and pulmonary vein arrhythmogenesis, further highlighting the interdependence between cardiac and pulmonary physiology. Furthermore, dysregulation of the apelinergic pathway has been implicated in the pathophysiology of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) [4], while latent class analysis reveals heterogeneity in PAH subtypes associated with congenital heart disease [2]. These findings underscore the importance of considering both cardiac and pulmonary function when understanding the complex interactions within the heart-lung axis.

Heart|Thyroid.description: The Heart-Thyroid axis is a complex interplay between the heart and thyroid gland, mediated by key signalling molecules such as thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) [1] and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) [2]. In response to TSH, the thyroid gland secretes triiodothyronine (T3), which in turn increases cardiac contractility and reduces peripheral resistance, as seen in low T3 syndrome in heart failure [3]. Conversely, hypothyroidism can lead to cardiac tamponade due to pericardial effusion, a condition exacerbated by the loss of thyroid hormone-induced ion channel function, including HCN and Kv channels [4]. The axis is further modulated by TRH, which stimulates the release of norepinephrine from the adrenal medulla, increasing heart rate and blood pressure [5].

Liver|Spleen.description: The liver-spleen axis is mediated by complex interplay of hormonal and metabolic signals, with the liver playing a central role in regulating splenic function. The release of bile acids from the liver acts as a key signaling molecule, binding to specific receptors on splenic macrophages, thereby modulating their polarization and immune response [1]. Conversely, the spleen produces various cytokines and chemokines that are released into the circulation, influencing liver metabolism and function [2]. The balance between these opposing signals is crucial for maintaining homeostasis in this axis, with disruptions leading to various pathological conditions such as gastralgia and chronic fatigue syndrome [3,4].

Muscle|Pancreas.description:
The Muscle-Pancreas axis is a critical inter-organ communication network where skeletal muscle plays a vital role in regulating pancreatic function and metabolism [2]. The release of myokines, such as fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) and irisin, from skeletal muscle stimulates the pancreas to produce hormones that regulate glucose and lipid metabolism [3]. In response, the pancreas produces incretins, such as GLP-1 and GIP, which stimulate insulin secretion in the liver and peripheral tissues [4]. Disruption of this axis, as seen in pancreatic cancer, can lead to muscle wasting and impaired pancreatic function, contributing to disease progression [5].

Note: I've focused on the most important signalling molecules and mechanisms, such as myokines, incretins, and their interactions with the pancreas and skeletal muscle.

Muscle|Thyroid.description: Thyroid hormone (TH) plays a critical role in regulating skeletal muscle physiology, influencing both contractile function and metabolic pathways. Through the regulation of ion channels, such as voltage-gated potassium channels [1], TH modulates muscle excitability and contraction. Additionally, TH signaling creates an intracellular environment conducive to protein accretion and oxidative capacity, supporting mitochondrial integrity and coordinated protein turnover [2]. This hormonal axis is further supported by the clinical efficacy of parathyroid autotransplantation into skeletal muscle during thyroid surgery, suggesting a functional restoration mechanism [3].

Muscle|WAT.description: The Muscle-WAT axis is regulated by a complex interplay between skeletal muscle and visceral adipose tissue (VAT), mediated by key signalling molecules such as Hedgehog pathway ligand Desert Hedgehog [1], which promotes myofiber repair and suppresses intramuscular adipogenesis. In contrast, inflammation and aging acceleration, linked to poor sleep quality, inversely associate with the skeletal muscle mass-to-visceral fat ratio (SVR) [2]. The gut microbiome and circulating metabolites also play a crucial role in modulating body composition, as evidenced by studies linking cancer cachexia to depletion of both skeletal muscle and adipose tissue [3]. Furthermore, metabolic flexibility and oxidative metabolism in skeletal muscle and brown adipose tissue can be enhanced by extracts from purple sweet potato leaves, which may prevent weight gain and lipotoxicity [4], while muscle-derived ANXA2 promotes hepatic steatosis through activation of SREBP1c-mediated de novo lipogenesis [5].

Pancreas|Thyroid.description: The pancreas-thyroid axis is a complex interplay between metabolic and hormonal signals that regulate glucose homeostasis and pancreatic function. Thyroid hormones, particularly T3, play a crucial role in modulating pancreatic beta-cell function and insulin sensitivity [1, 2]. Elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels have been linked to insulin resistance and beta-cell dysfunction in type 2 diabetes with subclinical hypothyroidism [4], while genetic liability to hypothyroidism has been shown to protect against pancreatic disease risk [3]. Furthermore, dietary dityrosine, a biomarker of high-oxidative pork consumption, can disrupt thyroid hormone signaling in pancreatic beta-cells, impairing glucose homeostasis [5].

Pancreas|WAT.description: The Pancreas-WAT axis is orchestrated by the IL-1β/CXCL12 signalling pathway, which promotes crosstalk between pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PanNETs) and adipocytes [1]. This axis is also linked to impaired autophagic flux in adipose tissue, exacerbating pancreatic injury in obesity-related severe acute pancreatitis [4]. Furthermore, tumour-infiltrating adipocyte-derived 12,13-DiHOME can subvert CD8+ T cell immunity in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma by promoting PPARγ-mediated ferritinophagy and tumour-associated neutrophil ferroptosis [3]. The interplay between these mechanisms highlights the complex relationships between adipose tissue, PanNETs, and pancreatic function.

Small Intestine|Spleen.description: The Small Intestine-Spleen axis is a bidirectional communication network where the gut microbiome and the spleen interact to regulate systemic homeostasis [1]. The gut microbiota produces short-chain fatty acids, which are then absorbed by the splenic endothelial cells, triggering the release of splenic hormones such as sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) and adrenomedullin, which in turn modulate immune responses and inflammation [2]. Additionally, the spleen produces cytokines that can influence gut barrier function and intestinal epithelial cell proliferation, highlighting a complex interplay between these two organs [3]. This axis is also influenced by external factors such as diet and lifestyle, with fermented foods like Polygonatum sibiricum and Poria cocos shown to modulate the gut-spleen axis and prevent spleen deficiency constipation [2].

Thyroid|WAT.description: The Thyroid-WAT axis is mediated by thyroid hormones, which regulate brown adipogenesis through the activation of uncoupling protein 1 [4]. Fructose consumption impairs brown adipogenesis by promoting thyroid hormone resistance in differentiated brown adipocytes [1], suggesting a link between excessive sugar intake and metabolic dysfunction. Additionally, adipocytes can promote tumor cell invasion and metastasis via FATP2, highlighting a novel cell-cell interaction in papillary thyroid carcinoma [3]. The differential effects of EP3, FP, and EP2 receptor agonists on orbital adipogenesis in a 3D spheroid model of thyroid eye disease further underscore the complex interplay between thyroid hormones and adipose tissue [2].
